newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rejects peace talks, says send refugees home.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rejects peace talks, says send refugees home.

text.p: Zaire, which accuses Rwanda of fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in the east, ruled out peace talks on Saturday while foreign troops remained on its soil and said refugees should be progressively forced to leave.
Spokesman Boguo Makeli told state television the government had decided a series of measures late on Friday including the closure of Zaire's eastern borders with Rwanda, Burundi and part of Uganda.
He highlighted what he called the government's "categorical refusal to take part in any meeting of any kind on the events in the east until the aggressors have left for good".
A European Union envoy, Aldo Ajello, told Reuters after two days in Kinshasa that he had so far failed to persuade the Zairean government to attend talks.
"We are working to create the conditions for a meeting to take place, but we have not yet got Zaire's agreement," Ajello, the EU Great Lakes envoy, said.

He said efforts were being made to persuade Rwanda and Zaire to meet informally at the next meeting of the Arusha Club, which groups regional governments party to the economic sanctions on Burundi imposed after a military coup there last July.
Zaire is the latest victim of bitter Hutu-Tutsi rivalry which has poisoned life in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi for generations.
Over a million Hutu refugees have lived in camps in eastern Zaire since 1994 when they fled Rwanda fearing reprisals or an upsurge in civil war after the genocide of Tutsis there.
"The real problem is what we do with the Hutu refugees and the military presence among them," Ajello said.
He said Tutsi-led Rwanda saw the presence of Hutus blamed for the 1994 genocide as a security threat.

"(Rwandan Vice-President and Defence Minister Major) General (Paul) Kagame has been asking the international community to solve this problem and warning that if they didn't, he would," he said, adding that he did not believe Rwanda had any long-term territorial ambitions in eastern Zaire.
Around 200,000 Burundian Hutu refugees are also in Zaire, having fled ethnic violence and war at home. Tens of thousands of Zaireans have been uprooted by the fighting in the east.
Boguo said the government had decided that there should be a "forced and progressive expulsion of all the Rwandan Hutu refugees" camped on Zairean territory.
"In this connection, the governmeent is keen to inform international opinion that if (protective) corridors must be created to settle the refugees, it's in Rwanda that they must be set up," he said.
He said the government had invited the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees to stop sending food aid to Zaire and send it to Rwanda and Burundi instead.
Boguo said the refugee town of Bukavu was back in Zairean army hands "apart from pockets of resistance observed here and there". Journalists in the town say the rebels are in control.
